org.portico.container

Interface IDaemon


  • public interface IDaemon
    NOTE: For automatic configuration by the Portico framework, all Daemons should declare the Daemon annotation. Further, all implementations should have a no-arg constructor so that instances can be created via reflection.

    In Portico, a IDaemon represents some process of component that needs to run inside the local Container. This is just a generic facility to allow additional behaviour to be plugged into the Portico infrastructure. Whether that behaviour has anything to do with the HLA is of no concern to the rest of the framework. A IDaemon can really be used for any purpose. To give you some examples (and hopefully set your mind wandering for new ideas), here are some possible examples:

    • Embed a Web Server to serve content from
    • A "keep alive" daemon that sends a heartbeat to the RTI at regular intervals
    • An IRC bot reporting on the status of various internal components
    • A federation bridge that can send messages back and forth between federations
    • A GUI displaying federation statistics or LRC loaded
    • etc... anything you can come up with!
    As you can see, some of these have a direct relation to the HLA, while others have nothing to do with it at all. Remember, a IDaemon is just a generic process that is associated with a Container.

    Daemon Configuration

    Configuration information should generally be passed to a IDaemon via java system properties. This is the highly recommended way for a IDaemon to extract its configuration information, as it means that any data provided in a RID file will be available. In Portico, a RID file is just a java properties file. On startup, all the properties are read in and registered as system properties. As configuration via a RID file is the most common way to provide HLA RTI configuration data, it is strongly suggested that you use system properties for IDaemon configuration.

    If your Daemon has more elaborate configuration needs, it is suggested that you read your configuration from a seprate file (formatted however you like it), but that you get the location of that file from a system property. Remember, when getting the value for a system property, you can specify a default value to use if that property isn't set (an excellent way to apply defaults). The PorticoConstants class has some examples of this (the DEFAULT_TIMEOUT static variable being one), so see the code for that class if you want an example.

    Daemons and Threading

    All IDaemon lifecycle methods are expected to return in a timely fashion. Thus, if your daemon implementation requires ongoing processing to occur, it will have to start a separate thread during the startDaemon() call for this work to run in (and stop/clean up that thread during the stopDaemon() call).

    New LRC notification

    The group of IDaemons exists inside a Container. However, all the interesting activity is going on down at the LRC level. It is for this reason that each Daemon will be notified whenever a new LRC is created and linked into a container. The Daemon can then take whatever action it needs to hook into the LRC.

    • Method Detail

      • getName

        String getName()
        Each type IDaemon should have a unique, identifiable name. Generally speaking, this method can be implemented as a simple return "ircbot";, where "ircbot" is the name of the Daemon. This name is generally used in logging and other reporting.

      • setName

        void setName(String name)
        This should only be called by the Portico framework. The name given to a Daemon will be the value extracted from the Daemon class-level annotation. If no name is provided in that annotation, the name of the implementation class (non-qualified) will be used.

      • isActive

        boolean isActive()
        This method should return true if the IDaemon is active and running, false otherwise.

      • configure

        void configure(Container container)
        throws JConfigurationException
        This method is called before either of the other lifecycle methods and gives the Daemon a chance to configure itself. For more information on the recommended approach for obtaining configuration information from a user, see the class level comment here. The Container used as a parameter is the Container in which the Daemon is registered.
        Throws:
        JConfigurationException

      • startDaemon

        void startDaemon()
          throws Exception
        When the Container is ready, it will start the IDaemons contained within it. At that time, this method will be called. Daemon implementations should take this opportunity to start any threads they need to complete their work, or generally kick off whatever is in need of kicking. The Daemon is expected to return from this method in a timely fashion, so it cannot use the current thread to perform any ongoing work.
        Throws:
        Exception

      • stopDaemon

        void stopDaemon()
         throws Exception
        On Container shutdown, this method will be called to notify the IDaemon that processing is over and it is time to exit. Implementations should take this opportunity to kill any worker threads they have running, close any connections they have open, and do any general cleanup that is necessary.
        Throws:
        Exception

      • lrcCreated

        void lrcCreated(LRC lrc)
        When the Container starts a new LRC, this method will be called on all the IDaemons, giving them access to it. The Daemon can then store it for later use or hook into it as required.

      • lrcDestroyed

        void lrcDestroyed(LRC lrc)
        Informs the IDaemon that the previously started LRC has become inactive and has been removed from the Container. The Daemon should now remove any storage it has relating to the lrc and break all links. It's dead. It's time to move on.
